subject: chemistry-hl
topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
choices: Forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant
The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped completely
The concentrations of reactants and products are always equal
The forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction
items.note: Both reactions continue at the same rate in a closed system; concentrations stop changing but need not be equal.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: Which is the equilibrium expression for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
items.note: Products over reactants, each concentration raised to its coefficient.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: A catalyst added to a system at equilibrium will:
choices: Shift the equilibrium towards the products
Shift the equilibrium towards the reactants
Not change the position of equilibrium
items.note: It speeds up forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position and K are unchanged.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0, which change increases the equilibrium yield of SO₃?
items.note: 3 mol gas → 2 mol gas: higher pressure favours fewer moles. Higher T favours the endothermic (reverse) direction.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: For an exothermic forward reaction, increasing the temperature:
choices: Does not change the value of K
items.note: K depends only on temperature. Heating favours the endothermic direction, here the reverse, so K falls.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: A large value of Kc (e.g. 10¹⁰) indicates that:
choices: The equilibrium lies far to the right
The reaction has a large activation energy
The equilibrium lies far to the left
items.note: K tells you the extent of reaction, not the rate. K ≫ 1 → mostly products.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the equilibrium concentrations are [H₂] = 0.10, [I₂] = 0.10, [HI] = 0.70 mol dm⁻³. Kc is:
items.note: Kc = 0.70² ÷ (0.10 × 0.10) = 0.49 ÷ 0.010 = 49 (no units, as moles of gas are equal on both sides).

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: For a reaction with Kc = 49, a mixture has reaction quotient Q = 10. The reaction will:
choices: Proceed in reverse until Q = Kc
Stay unchanged because the system is at equilibrium
items.note: Q < K → too few products, so net forward reaction until Q rises to K.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: If Kc for A ⇌ 2B is 4.0, what is Kc for 2B ⇌ A?

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: 1.00 mol H₂ and 1.00 mol I₂ are placed in a 1.00 dm³ flask; Kc = 49 for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. What is [HI] at equilibrium?

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: ΔG° = −RT ln K. A reaction with K = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ at 298 K has:
choices: A negative ΔG°, so products are favoured
A positive ΔG°, so reactants are favoured
ΔG° = 0, as K is very small
A positive ΔG°, so it can never occur
items.note: ln K < 0 → ΔG° > 0 (≈ +28.5 kJ mol⁻¹). Some products still form; the equilibrium simply lies to the left.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: State and explain the effect of increasing pressure on N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
markscheme: Equilibrium shifts to the right / more NH₃ (1)
Right side has fewer gas moles (2 vs 4) (1)
System opposes the change by reducing the pressure (Le Châtelier) (1)
items.tactic: Pressure: count gas moles on each side, then apply Le Châtelier.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: Explain why industrial ammonia production uses a moderate temperature (about 450 °C) even though the forward reaction is exothermic.
markscheme: Lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield (1)
But the rate would be too slow at low temperature (1)
450 °C is a compromise between yield and rate (with a catalyst) (1)
items.tactic: Compromise questions: yield argument, rate argument, then the conclusion.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem: 0.200 mol of PCl₅ is placed in a 1.00 dm³ container: PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g). At equilibrium, 0.050 mol of Cl₂ is present. Calculate Kc.
markscheme: Equilibrium: PCl₅ 0.150, PCl₃ 0.050, Cl₂ 0.050 mol dm⁻³ (1)
items.tactic: ICE table: Initial, Change (using the mole ratio), Equilibrium — then substitute.

items.topicLabel: R2.3 How far? The extent of chemical change
items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) For an invented gas-phase reaction X ⇌ Y, the % of Y at equilibrium was measured: 300 K 80%; 400 K 62%; 500 K 41%.
(a) Deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic, with a reason. (b) Calculate Kc at 400 K. (c) Predict the effect on Kc of adding a catalyst at 400 K.
markscheme: Yield of Y falls as temperature rises, so the reverse (endothermic) direction is favoured at high T (1)
(c) No change in Kc (equilibrium reached faster) (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
